purpose: Decode-only scoring of the two Cameroon pilot models on the frozen pilot test split. Diagnostic only: neither model is a promotion candidate and the 20% relative-WER nomination gate is deliberately NOT applied.

cm-base.init: BASE_INIT_CONTROL — pinned image predates warm-start support (commit 2de8a58); no STUDENT_WARM_START_LOADED line exists in its stream, which is the intended control

identical_training_config.CORRECTION_no_replay: An earlier version of this record claimed seven-language replay. That is FALSE. Both packets set MEDZEN_LANGUAGES=ngiemboon,ngombala,yangben,gbaya and both logs report 'manifests 4 at version cp1; eligible rows 10731'. Replay was in the plan; it was never in these runs.
identical_training_config.CORRECTION_not_only_init: An earlier version claimed the runs differ ONLY in initialisation. That is FALSE. They ran on different trainer images (4a7c1663 vs 059f4bfb) and therefore different code, including different RNG consumption before LoRA init. Initialisation and image are fully confounded; no clean single-variable contrast exists in this pair.

scoring.row_schema_note: v1/v2 used audio_s3_uri, copied from the omniasr_score.py module docstring. The evaluator actually reads row['audio_filepath'] (pipeline/omniasr_data.py:35). v3 matches the working Arm-2 manifest exactly: {audio_checksum_sha256, audio_filepath}.
scoring.uncertainty: corpus-level ratio bootstrapped over utterances, 2000 draws for absolute rates and 4000 for paired deltas, fixed seeds; NOT a mean of per-utterance rates

surfaces.cv_test: Common Voice 26.0 held-out test — IN-DOMAIN, speaker- and prompt-disjoint
surfaces.soreva: SOREVA — OUT-OF-DOMAIN directional metric, single speaker, short utterances; gbaya here is the CAR variety and is not decisive on its own

verdict: PRIMARY RESULT, and the only comparison this design supports: on these exact 1,419 in-domain clips, pooled word error moved +0.09 pp under the warm-started run (speaker-clustered 95% CI -0.40 to +0.55, 20 speakers). No pooled in-domain advantage was detected. The null holds under a corrected normaliser too (-0.04 pp).

That is NOT an answer to the initialisation question. The two runs used different trainer images and therefore different code and different RNG consumption before LoRA init, so initialisation is confounded with the image. This is a single-seed, cross-image diagnostic.
Neither run used replay. Both trained on the four Cameroon languages only.
Out of domain nothing is resolvable: SOREVA carries one speaker per language.
The raw counts reproduce exactly and independently: roughly 38-42% WER in domain on Ngiemboon, Ngombala and Gbaya, about 67% on Yangben, 80-90% out of domain, 10-14% in-domain character error.

But those are TONE-INSENSITIVE figures and they are FLOORS. The canonical scorer destroys every combining mark that cannot precompose — 4,240 across the reference set — which both splits words and hands the model free credit for tone errors. Tone-sensitive in-domain pooled figures are about 48.4% WER and 13.7% CER.

Tone is a large and language-dependent share of word error: at least 32.4% for Ngiemboon and 23.3% for Ngombala under the canonical tokenization, and 41.7% and 37.4% under a mark-preserving one, against roughly 12% for Yangben and Gbaya.
implication: The initialisation question is UNRESOLVED and this pilot cannot settle it. Do not treat base init as established or as safer. For the next real candidate: warm-start from Arm-1, actually replay the existing seven languages, train with the four Cameroon languages, and evaluate all eleven on a SINGLE image. Direct new data at Yangben and Gbaya, whose error is largely segmental. Fix the normaliser's mark handling and declare a tone policy BEFORE gating any of these languages — the current metric is tone-blind, flatters every model by roughly 6 WER points in domain, and distorts the ranking between the four languages.
not_applied: promotion, registry write, or deployment of either model
any claim that the initialisation question has been answered

error_decomposition_in_domain.SUPERSEDES: Two earlier versions of this section were wrong. (1) The first compared WER before and after STRIPPING combining marks; that changes the tokenization, so the rates had different denominators — 'pooled 42.6 -> 33.3' and '22% of word errors are tone' are withdrawn. (2) The second claimed the scorer defect INFLATES absolute WER and leaves CER untouched. Both halves are backwards, and the reason is that 'strip the marks' is not the counterfactual — 'keep the marks' is.

the_defect.what: services/asr-eval-runtime/medzen_asr_eval/metrics.py normalize_text maps every character that is not alphanumeric, whitespace or an apostrophe to a SPACE. A combining mark with no precomposed NFC form survives NFC with category Mn, is not alphanumeric, and is therefore replaced by a space. This both SPLITS THE WORD and DESTROYS THE MARK.
the_defect.selective: Precomposed vowels (i-acute, a-acute, a-caron, e-circumflex) are single alphanumeric codepoints and survive intact. The loss falls on exactly the vowels these orthographies need outside Latin-1 — schwa, open-o, barred-u, open-e — where the mark cannot precompose.

direction_CORRECTED.counterfactual: A mark-PRESERVING normaliser: identical to the canonical one except that category Mn characters are kept and stay attached to their base letter. Deleting the marks instead is not a fix — it is the same information loss without the word split, and it reproduces the canonical numbers exactly.
finding: The canonical scorer is OPTIMISTIC, not inflationary. Destroying the marks gives the model free credit for every tone error it makes, and that effect dominates the opposing effect of the inflated word denominator.
Every reported WER and CER in this record is therefore a FLOOR. The tone-sensitive in-domain pooled figures are about 48.4% WER and 13.7% CER, against the 42.6% and 11.5% reported.

CER is NOT immune. Reference characters rise 8.2% under the fix (46,144 -> 49,938) because the canonical scorer loses exactly one character per destroyed mark. In relative terms CER moves MORE than WER.
The canonical metrics are best described as TONE-INSENSITIVE WER and CER, and should be labelled that way.
direction_CORRECTED.cross_language_warning: Inflation ranges from 9.0% to 18.2%, so the four canonical WERs are not comparable with each other, nor with externally published WER for these languages.

robustness_of_the_primary_result.note: The warm-versus-base comparison is NOT affected by any of this — both arms are scored identically.
robustness_of_the_primary_result.conclusion: The null holds under both normalisers.

tone_share_of_word_errors.method: Align reference and hypothesis word sequences under ONE tokenization, then count substitutions whose two words are identical after removing combining marks. Denominator is the scorer's own word_errors under that same tokenization.
tone_share_of_word_errors.caveat: The canonical figures are floors: tone carried on a non-precomposing vowel is deleted before alignment, so those errors can never appear as a tone-only substitution. The earlier reading that Gbaya has essentially no tone problem (5.0%) is an artifact — under the mark-preserving tokenization Gbaya is 11.4% and Yangben 12.2%, a near-tie.
tone_share_of_word_errors.surviving_ordering: Ngiemboon and Ngombala carry far more tone error than Yangben and Gbaya under BOTH tokenizations.

uncertainty_correction.problem: The originally reported intervals bootstrapped over UTTERANCES. Utterances are clustered within speakers, so those intervals are too narrow and no significance claim derived from them is sound.

soreva_pooled.caveat: 4 clusters — the interval is reported for completeness and is not a basis for a claim

speaker_clustered_paired_delta_warm_minu.per_language: NOT ESTIMABLE. 1 speaker per language on SOREVA; 3-9 in domain, where a cluster bootstrap is degenerate and produced unstable intervals in both directions.

withdrawn_claims: 'Ngombala out of domain is significantly worse under the warm start' — rests on a single speaker.
'Pooled out-of-domain character error is significantly worse' — rests on 4 speakers; too fragile to assert.
Every per-language significance statement, in both directions.
